opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the single most important thing is realizing that a paper is a communication device, not a lab notebook. A lot of researchers, especially early on, structure their paper the way they experienced the research: "First we tried this, then we noticed that, then we ran this other thing." But the reader doesn't care about your journey. They care about what's true now and why they should believe it.

The way I like to frame it is that a good paper has a narrative. Concretely, that means something like one to three key claims. If you can't state the contribution in a couple of sentences, you probably don't yet know what your paper is about, and the reader definitely won't figure it out for you. So step one, before you write anything, is to sit down and write out: what are the claims, and what's the evidence for each? Everything in the paper should be in service of that. If an experiment doesn't support or contextualize one of the claims, it goes in the appendix or it gets cut, however much work it took.

Then I think you want to front-load ruthlessly. Most people will read the title, maybe the abstract, maybe glance at figure one, and that's it. So the abstract should state the claims plainly, the introduction should basically be a summary of the whole paper, with the key results stated up front, and figure one should ideally convey the core idea on its own. Contribution bullet points at the end of the intro are great, they're slightly formulaic, but they force you to be crisp.

Another thing that matters a lot is calibration. Be clear about how confident you are in each claim and what the evidence actually shows versus what you suspect. In interpretability especially, it's really easy to tell a compelling story that the evidence only weakly supports. Readers remember a paper better and trust it more if you say, "this is the thing we're confident in, here's the thing that's suggestive, here are the limitations." Paradoxically, being honest about weaknesses makes the strong parts land harder.

And finally, iterate with real readers. Give a draft to someone who wasn't involved and ask them afterward, "What do you think the main claims were?" If what they say back doesn't match what you intended, that's not their fault, that's a writing bug. I find that exercise catches more problems than almost anything else.

r001.rationale: The response says readers care about what is true and criticizes recounting the research journey, but does not say prolonged immersion causes researchers to overestimate how clear the paper will be.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking an uninvolved reader to identify the main claims and says mismatches reveal a writing bug, but does not recommend prioritizing revisions based on that feedback.

r003.rationale: It recommends structuring the paper around one to three key claims and putting everything in service of those claims, rather than narrating every step of the research process.

r004.rationale: It recommends stating claims up front and summarizing the paper in the introduction, but does not recommend explaining the central ideas in detail before presenting detailed evidence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to internalize is that your paper is going to be read by busy people who are skimming. Most readers will read the title, maybe the abstract, maybe look at the first figure, and then decide whether to keep going. So the question you should be asking is: what is the one or two sentence takeaway I want someone to walk away with? And then the entire paper should be structured around hammering that home.

I think the biggest mistake I see, especially from junior researchers, is that they treat the paper like a lab notebook. Here's everything we did, in the order we did it, including the dead ends and the three slightly different experiments that all point in the same direction. And that's not what a paper is for. A paper is a piece of communication. Its job is to compress a lot of research into something that efficiently moves the reader's beliefs. The narrative of how you got there is usually irrelevant.

So concretely, I'd say: pick your core claim. Ideally one claim, maybe two or three if they're genuinely distinct. Then your abstract should state it clearly. Your introduction should motivate it, explain why someone should care, and preview the evidence. Figure one should ideally be the single most compelling piece of evidence for that claim, something someone can look at for thirty seconds and get the gist. And then the body of the paper is there to back it up in enough rigor that a skeptical expert is convinced.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that if you have a result that doesn't support the core narrative, you should seriously consider cutting it or putting it in an appendix. This feels painful because you did the work. But every extra thing you include dilutes the reader's attention. People remember papers with one clear idea. They do not remember papers with seven medium-sized ideas.

And honestly, I think a lot of this comes down to spending way more time on the writing than people instinctively want to. The research might be ninety percent of the effort, but if the paper is badly structured, most of the value just doesn't make it out into the world. So iterate on the abstract and intro a lot. Get people who haven't seen the work to read it and tell you what they think the main point is. If they get it wrong, that's a problem with the paper, not with them.

r001.rationale: The response says readers are busy and skim, but does not connect researchers’ prolonged immersion in a project with overestimating how clear the paper will be.

r002.rationale: It recommends having people unfamiliar with the work read the paper, using their understanding of its main point as feedback, and iterating on the abstract and introduction when they miss it.

r003.rationale: It says to organize the paper around one or a few core claims and contrasts that with recounting every step, dead end, and experiment.

r004.rationale: It recommends stating and motivating the claim in the introduction, but does not clearly recommend explaining the central ideas in detail before presenting detailed evidence.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to be clear about what you actually want the reader to take away. If they remember one thing from your paper a week later, what should it be? And then structure the paper around making that thing understandable and convincing.

The abstract should tell me what you found, rather than just tell me that you investigated an interesting question. The introduction should explain why I should care, what the contribution is, and enough of the intuition that I have a framework for understanding the evidence. Then the rest of the paper should substantiate those claims.

I think a common mistake is to write the paper in the order you did the research. You tried something, it didn’t work, you tried something else, and eventually you got somewhere interesting. But that’s often quite different from the order in which a reader needs to encounter the ideas.

And be explicit about what you haven’t shown. If I understand both the result and its limitations, I can actually use it. If I finish with a vague impression that you’ve done something impressive, but I can’t articulate what we now know that we didn’t know before, the paper hasn’t really succeeded at communicating its contribution.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention researchers’ prolonged immersion or overestimating how clear the paper will be to readers.

r002.rationale: It gives no recommendation to prioritize revisions based on confusion revealed by reader feedback.

r003.rationale: It says to structure the paper around the one thing readers should remember and warns against recounting the research process in the order it happened.

r004.rationale: It recommends explaining the contribution and enough intuition in the introduction to give readers a framework for understanding the evidence, before the rest of the paper substantiates the claims.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful thing is to ask, “What do I want someone to remember about this paper a month after reading it?” And then structure the paper around making that clear. It’s very easy to write a paper that reflects the order in which you did the research, but that’s often a pretty confusing order in which to explain it.

I’d want the introduction to tell me what the contribution is, why I should care, and what evidence supports it. Give me the punchline early. Don’t make it a mystery where I have to get to page seven before I understand what you actually found.

And then the rest of the paper should make that claim precise and let me assess whether it’s true. A good figure can do a lot of work here: ideally there’s something I can look at and go, “Oh, that’s the result.” You need the details and the caveats, but I should be able to tell which details are essential to the main argument and which are there for completeness.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention researchers’ prolonged immersion or how it can distort their sense of what readers will understand.

r002.rationale: It gives no recommendation to use reader feedback on ideas or drafts to prioritize revisions.

r003.rationale: It recommends structuring the paper around what readers should remember and giving the main contribution early, rather than following the order of the research.

r004.rationale: It recommends stating the contribution and supporting evidence early, but does not clearly say to explain central ideas in detail before presenting evidence in detail.
